notes: The spine is the question structure every composed worksheet shares. Tokens in braces ({customer}, {jobs}, {worker}, {org}, {system}) are replaced from the pack's vocabulary. listKey pulls checkbox options from pack.lists. Each question lists the tiers it appears in; questions with ids starting t1. are the spoken-register set for owner-operators. Packs may override any field of any question via pack.overrides[questionId].

parts.title: You and your work
parts.intro: A quick picture of your job so the rest of your answers have context.

questions.label: Who am I talking to?
questions.help: Your name and the name of the business.

questions.label: Who works with you, and who does what?
questions.help: Rough is fine. “Me and one {worker}. My wife does the books on Sundays.”

questions.label: What do you run the business on?
questions.help: Tap everything. Paper and your head count.

questions.label: Your name
Your role or title
questions.placeholder: e.g., Office manager, Dispatcher, Director of Operations

questions.label: {Org} name
Best email for follow-up questions
Which areas are you responsible for?
questions.help: Check everything that lands on your desk, even partly.

questions.label: How many people do you work with or supervise day to day?
questions.help: A rough number is fine. Say who: “6 {workers}, 1 installer, me and the owner in the office.”
questions.placeholder: e.g., 8 in the field, 2 in the office

questions.label: What systems and tools do you touch in a normal week?
questions.help: Tap everything you use, then add anything missing. The whiteboard and the group text count.

questions.label: Where do your hours actually go in a typical week?
questions.help: Rough buckets with hours. Don’t be precise — be honest. Include the things that don’t feel like “real work.”
questions.placeholder: e.g., Phones ~12 hrs · The board ~10 hrs · Invoicing ~6 hrs · Chasing parts and people ~5 hrs …

questions.label: When is your busy season, and what changes when it hits?
questions.help: What gets dropped, what gets worse, who gets added.

parts.title: The pain inventory
parts.intro: This is the most important part. List up to ten things from your last two working weeks that were slow, repetitive, error-prone, or just annoying. One per row. For each one, describe one specific occasion — what actually happened, not what usually happens.

rule.text: No solutions. Your rows may not contain the words app, software, system, automate, dashboard, or AI. If you start writing “we need something that…”, stop and write down what happened instead.

parts.aside: The richest ground is rarely the main event of your job. It’s the preparing, the checking, and the chasing around it.

questions.label: Walk me through yesterday. First call of the morning to the last thing you did before you quit.
questions.help: Just what happened. Don’t tidy it up.

questions.label: What did you type twice this week?
questions.help: Same information, two places. A text and an invoice. A notepad and QuickBooks. The board and the {customer}’s file.

questions.label: What’s in your head, your truck, or your phone that isn’t written down anywhere?
questions.help: The things that would be gone if you were out for two weeks.

questions.label: What did you chase this week?
questions.help: Money, parts, callbacks, permits, an answer from somebody.

questions.label: What went wrong last month that you had to apologize for?
questions.help: To a {customer}, a supplier, or your own crew.

questions.label: Ten things that cost you time in the last two weeks
questions.help: You don’t have to fill all ten. Five good rows beat ten vague ones.

columns.label: Time lost each time (hands-on, not waiting)

parts.title: Your spreadsheets and workarounds
parts.intro: Most of the real system lives in personal spreadsheets, notebooks, and habits. That isn’t a failure — it’s where the requirements are hiding. Tell me about yours.

questions.label: The spreadsheets, lists, and documents you maintain by hand
questions.help: The ones you built yourself, or inherited, because nothing else held the information.

columns.label: What it tracks
columns.placeholder: Every {customer} on a maintenance plan, renewal month…

columns.label: What goes wrong with it
columns.placeholder: Out of date the minute I…

questions.label: Where does the “real” information live — the place everyone would agree is the truth? And where does it actually get looked up?
questions.help: These are often two different places. Say both.

questions.label: What do you copy, re-type, or re-format from one place to another every week?
questions.help: Be literal: from which document, into which document, how many items.

questions.label: What do you have to check or double-check before you can move on — and what happens when you skip it?
questions.help: The checks you do because you’ve been burned before.

questions.label: What do you wait on or chase?
questions.help: Deposits, parts, permits, a signature, a {worker}’s paperwork, an answer from the owner…

questions.label: What would break if you were out for two weeks?
questions.help: The things only you know how to do are the things most worth writing down.

parts.title: Pick one, and dig
parts.intro: Look back at your inventory. Pick the one that costs you the most, that affects other people, and where the information already exists somewhere — an email, a form, a sheet. That’s the one worth building for first.

questions.label: Of everything you just told me, which one bugs you the most?
questions.help: One thing. The one you’d pay to make go away.
questions.placeholder: The one that bugs me most is…

questions.label: How much of your week does that one eat?
questions.help: A guess is fine. Hours, or “every night after dinner.”

questions.label: My #1 problem
My backup, if the first one turns out to be harder than it looks
Why this one?
questions.help: It costs you every week, it costs someone else, the information already exists as text somewhere…

questions.label: Why does it happen? Keep asking “because.”
questions.help: Go as deep as you can; three is fine. Two endings that mean you’re not done: “because the software is bad” (too vague — what specifically?) and “because that’s how the {org} is set up” (true, but nobody can build for it — back up one step).

questions.label: The root cause I’d want fixed
questions.help: One sentence. Pick the rung that someone could actually build for.

questions.label: Where in the job does the pain actually sit?
questions.help: Pick the one that fits best.
options: Figuring out what’s needed
“What does this {customer} actually want?”
Finding the information
“Which email had the model number?”
Getting inputs ready
“Cleaning up the {worker}’s notes before I can invoice”
Checking before you proceed
“Making sure the parts and labor are coded right”
Doing the main task
“Building the board for tomorrow”
Fixing when something changes
“The {customer} called and the part didn’t come in”
Watching that it worked
“Did the permit get filed? Did the renewal go out?”
Closing out
“Posting the invoice, closing the {job}, updating the sheet”
questions.note: If you picked “doing the main task,” look again. The main task usually goes fine — the pain is in getting ready, checking, and chasing around it. If it really is the main task, keep it.

parts.title: Walk me through it
parts.intro: For your #1 problem, tell me the story of one real time you did it, start to finish. Words are fine. Be literal about file names, who sent what, and where things end up.

questions.label: The trigger — what happens in the real world right before you start?
The input — the actual file, screen, email, form, or conversation
questions.help: Name it. Describe its format. Say how many items are in it, and how much it varies from one time to the next.

questions.label: What you do with it, step by step
questions.help: Number the steps. Include the parts that feel too obvious to mention — those are usually the parts that matter most.

questions.label: The output — what you produce, and where it lands
questions.help: Which screen, which sheet, which printout, which email — and who receives it. Not “on my screen.”

questions.label: Who checks or approves it, and who notices if it’s wrong?
What does a wrong answer look like? What does a missed item look like? Which is worse?
The numbers
questions.help: Best guesses are fine.

fields.label: How long it takes by hand today
How long to check one finished result

questions.label: Could you share 10–20 real examples of the input, and what the finished result should look like — with {customer} names and personal details removed?
questions.help: This matters more than anything else on this page. Real examples are how a builder learns what “right” looks like. Nothing gets built from invented data.
options: Yes, I can pull those together
Probably — I’d need to check with someone first
No, or not sure how

questions.label: If someone needs to okay that, who?

parts.title: Fit and guardrails
parts.intro: A few checks that save wasted weeks. Be honest — a “yes” here isn’t a bad thing. It changes what gets built, not whether.

questions.label: Are any of these true for your #1 problem?
questions.help: Check any that apply. Any check means the fix should draft and let a person decide, rather than act on its own.
options: The whole value is that it’s done exactly the same way every time (payroll, a price book, a permit form)
One mistake costs more than a hundred correct answers save (a wrong price to a {customer}, a wrong part on a truck, a missed safety step)
Someone must be able to see exactly why a result came out the way it did (an inspector, an auditor, the owner)
The people who do this task have said they don’t want it changed
It’s already fast and cheap, and a good-enough rule exists
The information never changes and there isn’t much of it

questions.label: Which of these describe the task?
questions.help: Check all that fit.
options: Reading or writing everyday language ({worker} notes, emails, forms, requests)
Sorting many varied items into your categories (every call, every request, every complaint)
Picking out the few that need attention from the many that don’t
Personalizing the same message for different {customers}
Matching two lists and flagging what differs (the receipt vs. the PO, the invoice vs. the {job})
Producing the same report or sheet from the same kind of file every week
Answering questions from a fixed set of documents (your price book, your policies, the manufacturer’s specs)
Predicting something that hasn’t happened yet (which estimates will close, which weeks will be short-staffed)

questions.label: The no-new-software answer: what’s the best fix that needs nothing built at all?
questions.help: A rule, a checklist, a template, a filter, a process change, asking someone. There almost always is one.

questions.label: Why isn’t that enough?
questions.help: If you can’t answer this, the no-software fix is probably the right first step — and that’s a fine outcome.

questions.label: Should the tool do it, or help you do it?
options: Do it, and I spot-check
Draft or suggest, and I decide every time
Not sure
questions.note: Rule of thumb: automate what’s tedious and agreed-on. Assist with what people enjoy, what carries relationships, or where people disagree about what “correct” means.

questions.label: Three quick ones

items.t: Do people agree on the correct way to do this task?
Are the stakes high for any single case?
Do people enjoy doing this task?

questions.label: Does the information involved include any of these?
questions.help: This decides how examples get shared and what a first version is allowed to touch.

questions.label: Who at your {org} needs to know or approve before anything runs on real information?
questions.placeholder: Name and role — or “nobody, it’s my call”

questions.label: Which systems would it need to touch — and could it be read-only?
questions.help: The safest first version reads from your systems and never writes into them. Is that workable here? What would it need to read?

parts.title: What “better” looks like
parts.intro: Now the outcome. Fill in the blanks in your own words — these two sentences become the first lines of the build.

questions.label: If that one went away, what would you do with the time?
questions.help: Be specific. “Quote the two jobs I never get to.” “Eat dinner with the kids.”

questions.label: Would you rather something does it and you check, or sets it up and you decide?
questions.help: Either answer is fine. It changes what gets built.
options: Does it, I check
Like a helper who finishes the paperwork and shows you
Sets it up, I decide
Like a helper who lays it out and waits for your OK
Not sure
We’ll figure it out on the call

questions.label: Anything you don’t want changed?
questions.help: The part of the job you like, or the thing you don’t trust anybody else with.

questions.label: The problem, in one sentence
The goal, in one sentence
How would you know it worked? Give me a number.
questions.help: “Invoices out the same day instead of three days later.” “Zero missed renewals this season.” “The board built by 4:30 instead of 6.”

questions.label: What should this NOT do?
questions.help: At least two things. Drawing the line is as useful as describing the goal.
questions.placeholder:
It should not… 
It should not…

questions.label: If it worked, what would you do with the time?
What would make you stop using it after a month?
Who else, by name or role, would use this or depend on it?
Which of these are true today?
questions.help: Each unchecked box is where a tool breaks first — and something to fix before or while building.
options: One named person would own this after it’s built, and it’s clear who
The information it needs lives in one place (not three spreadsheets and a group text)
The information arrives in a consistent format
There’s a written standard for what a “good” result looks like
Someone would look at a “not sure — needs a human” list every time it runs

questions.label: Anything else I should know?
questions.help: Busy seasons, staff turnover, the devices you use (a phone in the truck? a laptop in the office?), IT rules, budget, things that have been tried before and why they didn’t stick.

parts.title: Systems and data
parts.intro: Every system that touches your #1 problem. Be literal about who owns it and whether a first version could get away with only reading from it.

questions.label: The systems inventory
questions.help: One row per system, including the spreadsheets. “Owner” is the person who’d have to say yes to anything touching it.

columns.label: How data gets out
columns.placeholder: Nightly CSV export; API needs IT approval

questions.label: Where does the same number exist in more than one place — and which copy do people believe?
questions.help: This is usually where the pain lives at your size.

questions.label: What exports can you actually pull today, and who can pull them?
questions.help: CSV from a report, an accounting export, a scheduled email of a PDF — and whether it takes a request to someone else.

parts.title: People and constraints
parts.intro: Who decides, who’s affected, who’ll push back — and what the {org} requires before anything new runs.

questions.label: The people around this problem
questions.help: Include the person who’ll quietly ignore it. They matter most.

columns.label: Why
columns.placeholder: She was burned by the last rollout

questions.label: Which of these apply before anything new can run?
questions.help: Check all that apply. None of them stops the work; they change the order.

questions.label: Who owns this after it’s built?
questions.help: One name. If the answer is “whoever has time,” it will break within a month.

questions.label: The last time a new tool was rolled out here — what happened?
questions.help: Who adopted it, who didn’t, and why. This is the most predictive answer on the page.

parts.title: Success, and what to send
parts.intro: Numbers with a baseline, and the files that would save us both a week.

questions.label: Success metrics, with today’s number
questions.help: If nobody measures it today, say so — that’s useful too.

columns.label: Metric
columns.placeholder: Days from {job} complete to invoice sent

questions.label: Which of these could you send, with {customer} names and personal details removed?
questions.help: Last month’s exports are ideal — old enough to be safe, recent enough to be real. Email them to the address in the note that came with this link.

questions.label: Does your {org} need an NDA before we go further?
options: No
Yes — send one
Not sure, I’ll ask

parts.title: About this worksheet
parts.intro: You’re one of the first people to fill this out. Help me make it better for the next one — be blunt.

questions.label: Last one. How was this?
questions.help: Honest answer. It only gets better if you tell me.

fields.label: About how many minutes did it take?

questions.label: How long did this actually take you?
Was the length…
options: Too long
About right
Could be longer

questions.label: Which questions were confusing, hard to answer, or felt like the same question twice?
questions.help: Name them by part and wording if you can.

questions.label: Which questions felt pointless for your work?
What didn’t I ask that I should have?
Did the examples help, get in the way, or feel off for your world?
Rate this worksheet overall
Anything else?
